1.definition: A sailor's word for "in the middle of the ship" — the broad central section halfway between the bow and the stern, the steadiest part of a longship and where the heaviest cargo and the mast usually sat.

Of or belonging to Norway — here the mountainous, fjord-cut Atlantic flank of Scandinavia and its North Germanic farming-and-seafaring people, one of the three Norse populations from which the Viking raiders sailed.

2.definition: The shift from sailing home to Scandinavia each autumn to instead seizing a defensible river island or coastal fort and digging in for the winter, so a Viking fleet could raid from a fixed local base all year round.

3.definition: A town on the Yorkshire coast of England whose name ends in the Norse word -by ("village" or "farm"); its name is a lingering fingerprint of the Danelaw, the region Viking settlers controlled and renamed.
Of Norway — the people, language, and kingdom of the western Scandinavian coast, the homeland from which most of Iceland's settlers sailed.
Of Iceland — the North Atlantic island colony and the Old Norse dialect that, preserved in saga manuscripts, became the closest surviving relative of the language the Vikings spoke.

4.definition: Old Norse for "rowing men" — one proposed origin of the word Rus', describing the Swedish crews who plied the Russian river routes by drag-and-row.

5.definition: Old Norse "sitting out": a divination ritual where a seeker spent the night alone outdoors — often on a grave or at a crossroads — to reach the spirits or the dead and come back with hidden knowledge or a glimpse of the future.
A Norse spring sacrifice ("victory-blót") dedicated to Odin, performed at the start of the raiding season to beg the gods for triumph on the year's campaigns.
A midsummer Norse sacrifice dedicated to the fertility god Freyr, offered to secure a good harvest for the coming year.
The "Winter-Nights" sacrifice, held in October to mark the beginning of the winter half of the Norse year.
The midwinter Norse sacrifice from which the word Yule descends — the great pagan winter feast that Christianity later absorbed and rebranded as Christmas.

The community of western and central European lands under the Latin-rite, Rome-centered church — the "diplomatic club" a converting Norse king joined, distinct from the Greek Orthodox Byzantine world to the east.

With conversion came the Latin alphabet, which displaced runes for serious record-keeping — kings issued written charters and laws, and monasteries became the new centers of literacy across the Norse world.

6.definition: The dense, showy "lordly meter" of Viking court poetry: eight-line stanzas locked down by strict internal rhyme, alliteration, and syllable counts, and stuffed with riddling kennings. It was hard to compose and hard to follow — which was exactly the point, since pulling it off proved a skald's skill.

Old Norse for "head-ransom": a praise-poem a skald composed for a king who had him in his power, the verse literally buying back the poet's own neck. The most famous is the one Egil Skallagrímsson is said to have improvised overnight to flatter an enemy king out of executing him.
Old Norse for "the Great City" — the Viking name for Constantinople, the dazzling Byzantine capital that drew Swedish adventurers down the eastern rivers to serve, trade, and raid.

7.definition: The Scandinavian homeland (Denmark, Norway, Sweden) during the Viking Age, c. 793–1066 — the fjord-and-farm world whose trading towns, ring fortresses, and emerging kingdoms powered the diaspora.
Arabic-speaking peoples of the Islamic world; here the Andalusian merchant At-Tartushi, whose travelogue records a horrified outsider's look at the pagan trading town of Hedeby.
The Slavic peoples of eastern and central Europe, whose pottery, goods, and captives moved through Norse trade hubs like Birka along the river routes east.
Of Norway — here the Norwegian fleets and royal armies that, alongside Danish ones, mounted the second great wave of seaborne attacks on England.
Sister of Sweyn Forkbeard of Denmark, reportedly among the Danes killed in the St Brice's Day Massacre of 1002 — the act that helped trigger Sweyn's war of conquest against England.

8.definition: Followers of Christianity; here the Norse Normans who, three generations after Rollo, had become Christians and continental knights — the faith that reshaped the whole Norse world by 1066.
Followers of Islam; here the Muslim rulers of Sicily and southern Italy from whom Norman warlords seized those lands in 1060–1130.
